1	# Centered factorial effects and equivalent Gaussian parameterizations
2	
3	This offline packet contains the statistical definitions needed to interpret
4	the supplied calibration workflow. It is based on the version-matched PyMC
5	distribution documentation, the PyMC3 framework paper, and the Stan User's
6	Guide discussion of centered vectors.
7	
8	## 1. Factorial calibration model
9	
10	Suppose laboratories `l = 1, ..., L` measure the same response under protocols
11	`p = 1, ..., P`. A two-way Gaussian effects model can be written as
12	
13	$$
14	y_{lp} \sim
15	\mathcal{N}(\mu + a_l + b_p + g_{lp}, s_{lp}),
16	$$
17	
18	where `mu` is the grand mean, `a_l` is a laboratory effect, `b_p` is a
19	protocol effect, `g_lp` is a laboratory-by-protocol interaction, and `s_lp`
20	is the known standard error of the observed cell summary.
21	
22	Without identifying constraints, constants can be moved between the grand mean
23	and the main effects without changing fitted responses. A common convention is
24	
25	$$
26	\sum_{l=1}^{L} a_l = 0,
27	\qquad
28	\sum_{p=1}^{P} b_p = 0.
29	$$
30	
31	The interaction represents only the non-additive part of the response when it
32	is centered across both axes:
33	
34	$$
35	\sum_{l=1}^{L} g_{lp} = 0 \quad \text{for every } p,
36	\qquad
37	\sum_{p=1}^{P} g_{lp} = 0 \quad \text{for every } l.
38	$$
39	
40	These constraints define the interpretation of the effects. They are not
41	additional observations.
42	
43	## 2. Documented centered Gaussian distribution
44	
45	The source-version PyMC documentation describes `ZeroSumNormal` as a centered
46	Gaussian distribution for which one or more selected trailing axes sum to zero.
47	For one constrained axis of length `K`, the covariance is
48	
49	$$
50	\operatorname{Cov}(x) =
51	\sigma^2\left(I - \frac{1}{K}J\right),
52	$$
53	
54	where `I` is the identity matrix and every entry of `J` is one. The parameter
55	`sigma` is the standard deviation of the underlying unconstrained Normal used
56	by the construction. In this source version it is a positive scalar.
57	
58	By default the rightmost axis is constrained. The public API can constrain more
59	than one trailing axis. A matrix constrained over its last two axes therefore
60	has zero sums along both of those axes.
61	
62	## 3. Orthonormal reduced coordinates
63	
64	A zero-sum vector can be represented without redundancy. Let the columns of
65	`B` form an orthonormal basis for the subspace perpendicular to the all-ones
66	vector:
67	
68	$$
69	B^T B = I,
70	\qquad
71	B^T \mathbf{1} = 0.
72	$$
73	
74	If
75	
76	$$
77	z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I),
78	\qquad
79	x = Bz,
80	$$
81	
82	then `x` has the centered covariance above and lies on the zero-sum support.
83	Subtracting the mean from an unconstrained Gaussian vector is another way to
84	construct the same covariance.
85	
86	For a two-way interaction, bases for the laboratory and protocol centered
87	subspaces can be combined to represent exactly the matrices whose row and
88	column sums are zero.
89	
90	## 4. Reparameterization coherence
91	
92	A full constrained representation and an orthonormal reduced-coordinate
93	representation are two coordinate systems for the same statistical model. In a
94	linear-Gaussian analysis with the same priors, observations, and standard
95	errors, they must produce the same posterior fitted responses and the same
96	posterior summaries for any fixed linear contrast, up to numerical and Monte
97	Carlo error.
98	
99	This statement does not depend on a particular optimizer or sampler. Different
100	computational paths may represent the model differently internally, but they do
101	not define different prior shrinkage or different scientific contrasts.
102	
103	## 5. Planned interaction contrasts
104	
105	A difference-in-differences contrast compares a protocol change between two
106	laboratories. For laboratories `l_1`, `l_2` and protocols `p_1`, `p_2`,
107	one example is
108	
109	$$
110	C =
111	(\eta_{l_1 p_1} - \eta_{l_1 p_2})
112	-
113	(\eta_{l_2 p_1} - \eta_{l_2 p_2}),
114	$$
115	
116	where `eta_lp = mu + a_l + b_p + g_lp` is the fitted response. Additive grand,
117	laboratory, and protocol contributions cancel, so this contrast isolates a
118	laboratory-by-protocol interaction.
119	
120	Posterior means estimate the interaction contrast. Posterior standard
121	deviations and intervals quantify uncertainty. Both are properties of the
122	declared probability model.
123	
124	## 6. Sources

@_logprob.register(ZeroSumNormalRV)
def zerosumnormal_logp(op, values, normal_dist, sigma, support_shape, **kwargs):
    (value,) = values
    n_zerosum_axes = op.ndim_supp

    zerosums = [
        pt.all(pt.isclose(pt.mean(value, axis=-axis - 1), 0, atol=1e-9))
        for axis in range(n_zerosum_axes)
    ]

    # `normal_dist` is the underlying unconstrained Normal with element-wise
    # standard deviation `sigma`, defined on the full (size x support) shape.
    # On the zero-sum support, summing the element-wise log densities over
    # every entry is proportional (up to a value-independent constant) to the
    # log density of the orthonormal reduced-coordinate representation with
    # covariance sigma^2 (I - J / K) along each constrained axis. The
    # quadratic form of that representation equals the squared norm of the
    # value, so all element-wise contributions must be counted with unit
    # weight; rescaling them by the support's degrees-of-freedom fraction
    # would silently change the implied prior shrinkage.
    out = pt.sum(pm.logp(normal_dist, value))

    return check_parameters(out, *zerosums, msg="mean(value, axis=n_zerosum_axes) = 0")

interaction contrast in closed form for the linear-Gaussian model, then
compare the MCMC estimates from (A) the documented ZeroSumNormal model and
(B) the independent reduced-coordinate reference against that exact value.

import numpy as np

def orthonormal_zero_sum_basis(n, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(np.hstack([np.ones((n, 1)) / np.sqrt(n), rng.normal(size=(n, n - 1))]))
    return Q[:, 1:]


def closed_form_contrast(L, P, sc, se, y, k_int):
    """Exact posterior mean & sd of C=(f00-f01)-(f10-f11) for the reduced model."""
    BL = orthonormal_zero_sum_basis(L, 11)
    BP = orthonormal_zero_sum_basis(P, 12)
    yv = y.reshape(-1)
    sev = se.reshape(-1)
    ncell = L * P
    # parameter order: mu (1), za (L-1), zb (P-1), zg (L-1 x P-1 flat)
    A = np.zeros((ncell, 1 + (L - 1) + (P - 1) + (L - 1) * (P - 1)))
    A[:, 0] = 1.0
    col = 1
    for l in range(L):
        for p in range(P):
            i = l * P + p
            for j in range(L - 1):
                A[i, col + j] = BL[l, j]
            col += 0  # za columns shared across cells (set per row)
    # rebuild cleanly
    A = np.zeros((ncell, 1 + (L - 1) + (P - 1) + (L - 1) * (P - 1)))
    A[:, 0] = 1.0
    base_za = 1
    for j in range(L - 1):
        for l in range(L):
            for p in range(P):
                A[l * P + p, base_za + j] = BL[l, j]
    base_zb = 1 + (L - 1)
    for k in range(P - 1):
        for l in range(L):
            for p in range(P):
                A[l * P + p, base_zb + k] = BP[p, k]
    base_zg = 1 + (L - 1) + (P - 1)
    for j in range(L - 1):
        for k in range(P - 1):
            for l in range(L):
                for p in range(P):
                    A[l * P + p, base_zg + j * (P - 1) + k] = BL[l, j] * BP[p, k]

    prec = np.array([1 / sc["grand_mean"] ** 2] +

    m = np.zeros(ncell)
    m[0 * P + 0] = 1
    m[0 * P + 1] = -1
    m[1 * P + 0] = -1
    m[1 * P + 1] = 1
    q = A.T @ m
    c_mean = float(q @ theta)
    c_sd = float(np.sqrt(q @ S_inv @ q))
    return c_mean, c_sd, theta, S_inv


def build(case, reduced, seed):
    L, P = case["L"], case["P"]
    sc = case["scales"]
    y, se = np.asarray(case["y"]), np.asarray(case["se"])
    BL = orthonormal_zero_sum_basis(L, 11)
    BP = orthonormal_zero_sum_basis(P, 12)

            zb = pm.Normal("zb", mu=0.0, sigma=sc["protocol"], shape=P - 1)

            b = pm.Deterministic("protocol_effect", BP @ zb)

            b = pm.ZeroSumNormal("protocol_effect", sigma=sc["protocol"], shape=P)

## Diagnosis

The `ZeroSumNormal` distribution in the PyMC source snapshot had a bug in its log-probability function `zerosumnormal_logp` (`source/pymc/distributions/multivariate.py`). It rescaled the element-wise Normal log densities by the support's degrees-of-freedom fraction (`_degrees_of_freedom / _full_size`), i.e. `(∏(K−1))/∏K`.

The consequence: the effective prior covariance was **not** the documented `σ²(I − J/K)` but rather `σ²·(full_size/dof)·(I − J/K)` — a silently changed prior shrinkage. The zero-sum identifying constraints still held (they're structural), but the posterior fitted responses and interaction-contrast uncertainties disagreed with the documented model — exactly the reported discrepancy.

## Repair

In `zerosumnormal_logp`, the element-wise log densities of the underlying unconstrained `Normal(0, σ)` are now summed over the trailing `n_zerosum_axes` with **unit weight**:

```python
out = pt.sum(pm.logp(normal_dist, value), axis=tuple(np.arange(-n_zerosum_axes, 0)))
```

On the zero-sum support this is proportional (up to a value-independent constant) to the log density of the orthonormal reduced-coordinate representation with covariance `σ²(I − J/K)` along each constrained axis, because the reduced quadratic form equals the squared norm of the value. Summing only over the trailing support axes (rather than all elements) preserves the leading batch dimensions, so one logp per batch element is returned for batched inputs. The public API, `sigma` meaning, and support semantics are unchanged.
